respite

RES-pit -- shares a root with 'inspect,' meaning to look back. · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Respite is a short period of rest from something difficult.

The brief cease-fire offered exhausted villagers a rare respite from months of constant shelling.

Worked Example

After six straight hours answering phones during the storm, the call-center staff finally gets a fifteen-minute break to sit down and catch their breath.

That short pause from ongoing hardship is exactly what a respite is. Unlike 'ending,' which means something is over completely, respite is only ever temporary.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

breather: A breather is a casual, everyday word for a short rest -- you take a breather after climbing the stairs. A respite is more serious: relief from genuine hardship, pain, or pressure, and the word often sounds a little formal or literary.

intermission: An intermission is a scheduled, built-in break, like the pause between acts of a play -- expected and planned for. A respite is never on the schedule: it is a snatched stretch of relief from real hardship, welcome precisely because it was not guaranteed.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

ordeal: a painful or difficult experience with no relief

continuation: the act of something carrying on without stopping

Where it sits · how much relief the pause brings — lull → respite → reprieve

lull vs. respite: A lull is a bit milder than a respite -- a lull just means a temporary quiet, while respite specifically implies relief from something genuinely hard or painful.

reprieve vs. respite: A reprieve can feel like a stronger relief than a respite: respite suggests a short pause before hardship likely returns, while reprieve can suggest a longer or more decisive escape from it, even if only for now.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — re-

Prefix — re-: back (Latin)

Root — spite

Root — spite: to look (from Latin specere, 'to look' -- respectus, 'a looking back,' was reshaped by Old French respit into this spelling)

Put it together

Put it together: Respite comes from Latin respectus, 'a looking back, consideration': re- ('back') + spite (from specere, 'to look,' reshaped by Old French respit). A respite, at its root, comes from pausing to look back and reconsider before continuing -- the same root that appears as -spect- in inspect.

Use the root in a new word: inspect

Use the root in a new word: inspect: Mechanics inspect every part of the engine before clearing a plane for takeoff.
